cases.title: Malawi fertilizer subsidy removal
cases.point: Lilongwe District, in Malawi's central maize-growing plateau (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its agricultural sector credit (ASAC) capped the fertilizer subsidy at 30% in 1990/91, 25% in 1991/92 and 20% in 1992/93 (FAO). The Mail & Guardian reports the Bank pushed in the 1980s and 1990s to end fertilizer subsidies entirely.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: A University of Washington (EPAR) review says IMF and donor pressure for fiscal austerity led Malawi in 2001 to limit free inputs to the poorest farmers.

cases.conditions: FAO: under the ASAC credit the fertilizer subsidy could not exceed 30%, 25% and 20% in the three seasons from 1990/91, and total subsidy spending was capped at 2%, 1.6% and 1.3% of government spending. A Fertilizer Subsidy Removal Program then aimed at full removal by 1995/96. Later, under donor pressure, the universal Starter Pack of free seed and fertilizer (begun 1998) was cut back to a targeted program (Harrigan, Food Policy 2008).
cases.community: Researchers at the University of Florida (Gough et al., 2002) found fertilizer use 'has therefore dropped significantly since 1994'; in 1999/2000 a 50 kg bag of urea cost MK 825, and prices pushed smallholders to stop or sharply cut fertilizer use. In southern Malawi 40 to 60% of rural households went short of food for two to five months a year. Free packs fell from about 3 million a year to 1.5 million in 2001 and about 1 million in 2002 (Network Ideas). FAO calls the cut in free inputs a major factor in the fall in maize output in 2001/02. After a poor 2005 harvest, almost 5 million of 13 million people needed emergency food aid (New York Times, via World Hunger Education Service); IPS reported 4.7 million facing food shortages, citing official figures.
cases.killed_note: No death count tied to the subsidy cuts. Network Ideas cites reports of 500 to several thousand hunger deaths in 2002, a crisis also linked to the grain reserve sale (a separate card).
cases.outcome: From 2005 the government brought back deep fertilizer subsidies against donor advice. Farmers got coupons for two 50 kg bags at about one fifth of the market price. Maize output rose from 1.2 million tonnes in 2004/05 to 2.6 million in 2005/06 and 3.2 million in 2006/07 (EPAR); good rains also helped. By 2007 Malawi was selling maize to the World Food Programme and Zimbabwe. The World Bank said it was never opposed to subsidies as such (Network Ideas).

cases.title: Zambia 1995 mining laws and development agreements
cases.point: Kitwe, centre of the Copperbelt mining towns (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Reform of the Investment Act was a condition of the Bank's 1993 PIRC II loan; the 1995 Investment Act and Mines and Minerals Act followed (Fraser and Lungu, for Christian Aid).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Later Fund and Bank loans (ESAF, ESAC II and others) required the state mining firm ZCCM to be broken up and sold; HIPC debt relief from 1996 added leverage (Fraser and Lungu).

cases.conditions: Change the investment law as a condition of the World Bank's 1993 PIRC II loan, then unbundle and privatise ZCCM under later IMF and World Bank loans (Fraser and Lungu). The 1995 Mines and Minerals Act let the state sign secret 'development agreements' with each buyer.
cases.community: Royalties: the Act set 3% of net back value, but most buyers negotiated 0.6% of gross revenue. Mining tax was 25% against 35% for manufacturing, terms were frozen for 15 to 20 years, and firms were not liable for pollution above ZCCM's past discharge levels during those years. Mine jobs fell from about 31,000 when the first mine was sold in 1997 to 19,145 in 2001; the Chamber of Mines counted 19,900 direct jobs in 2004. About 45% of mine workers had no permanent contract by 2006, and contract workers were paid about half of Mopani's wage for the same work. Mine hospitals and anti-malaria spraying were cut; by 2004 about a quarter of recorded Copperbelt deaths were from malaria (all from Fraser and Lungu).
cases.suppression: Unions told Fraser and Lungu that firms dismissed members of shadow union committees, and contract workers were kept out of union representation.
cases.outcome: The agreements were kept from MPs, unions and regulators. Pambazuka reports exemptions covered customs duty to pollution penalties.

sources.title: For Whom the Windfalls? Winners and Losers in the Privatisation of Zambia's Copper Mines
sources.publisher: Fraser and Lungu, for Christian Aid / Civil Society Trade Network of Zambia (SOAS repository)

sources.title: Zambia: Riches to rags

cases.confidence_note: This card covers the 1995 law and the general terms given to all buyers. The sales of Konkola and Mopani have separate cards. Fraser and Lungu give two job series that do not match (45,000 in 1995 to 22,000 in one section; 31,000 in 1997 to 19,145 in 2001 in another).

cases.title: DR Congo 2002 Mining Code
cases.point: Kolwezi, heart of the Katanga copper and cobalt belt (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The code 'was based on a draft prepared under the auspices of the World Bank' (Radley, The Conversation). IPIS notes the code was drafted by the DRC with the Bank.

cases.conditions: A new mining code drafted with World Bank help to reopen industrial mining to foreign investors after the 1996-2003 wars (Radley; IPIS). Terms: 30% profit tax, 2% royalty on copper and cobalt, and a 5% free state share in new projects.
cases.community: A GIZ study found the state took only 6% of total mining-sector revenue in 2011-2014. Marysse and Tshimanga found an overall tax rate of 21% at one large copper mine, against the 46% the World Bank itself recommends (both cited by Radley). IPIS reports a gap of US$35 million in royalties and surface rents from fraud, and only about $27 million in sector taxes reported for 2005, against about $200 million that should have been due. Only three of the code's 344 articles deal with people living on mining concessions, giving little guidance on forced displacement (Radley). Amnesty International reports artisanal miners were moved off sites as companies moved in, 'sometimes violently'.
cases.suppression: Amnesty International reports threats, beatings and ill-treatment of artisanal miners by mine police and private guards in Katanga.
cases.outcome: In 2017 the government was revising the code; the draft raised copper and cobalt royalties from 2% to 3.5%, profit tax to 35% and the state share to 10% (Radley).

sources.title: The DRC is revisiting its mining code. Why reform is long overdue
sources.publisher: The Conversation (Ben Radley, Erasmus University Rotterdam)

sources.title: World Bank and DRCongo Mining Session, Paris
Profits and loss: Mining and human rights in Katanga

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's drafting role is documented. The harms shown are mainly lost public revenue and weak protection for people on concessions; Amnesty's evictions are not tied by Amnesty to the code itself.

cases.title: Tanzania Mining Act 1998
cases.point: Lake Victoria goldfields of northwest Tanzania (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its 1990 Mining Sector Review set the course for a Mineral Sector Development Strategy; the reviews leading to the 1998 Mining Act 'were financed by the World Bank' (Lissu, citing Mining Annual Review 1997).

cases.conditions: World Bank-funded review of the legal, regulatory and fiscal framework for mining, leading to the Mining Act, 1998 (Lissu, 2001).

companies.name: Barrick Gold
companies.role: Signed a 2007 contract that reportedly fixed tax levels for 25 years, renewable for 25 more (Curtis and Lissu, via IISD)

cases.community: Royalty on gold was 3%, and firms could write off 100% of capital spending. A 2003 audit (not public) reportedly found four companies over-declared losses by US$502 million in 1999-2003, a revenue loss of US$132.5 million; a 5% royalty would have raised about US$58 million more over five years (Curtis and Lissu, 2008). A peer-reviewed CMI study found government mining revenue below 5% of aid, legal protections for affected people not followed, and smallholders getting little or no compensation, or having it embezzled.
cases.outcome: After wide public anger, Tanzania amended the 1998 Act in 2010 (CMI). Barrick called the Curtis and Lissu report 'basically an advocacy piece'.

sources.title: In Gold We Trust: The Political Economy of Law, Human Rights and the Environment in Tanzania's Mining Industry
sources.publisher: Law, Social Justice & Global Development Journal (Warwick)

sources.title: Report says Tanzania is signing bad deals with foreign mining companies

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank financed the reviews behind the Act (Lissu), but no source opened here shows a loan condition requiring the Act. Harms documented are mainly lost revenue and poor compensation. The 1996 Bulyanhulu evictions came before this Act and are not counted here.

cases.title: Indonesia palm oil export ban lifted
cases.point: Medan, North Sumatra, a palm oil centre where riots in early May 1998 increased panic buying (CIFOR)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The January 15, 1998 Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies set the end of the palm oil export ban and the opening of plantations to foreign investors. CIFOR reports the IMF would not let the government bring the ban back.

cases.conditions: IMF memorandum of January 15, 1998: the palm oil export ban to be kept only through the first quarter of 1998, then replaced by export taxes 'at rates not exceeding 20 percent'; restrictions on foreign investment in palm oil plantations removed from February 1, 1998; all other export restrictions to go within three years.
cases.community: The government had banned crude palm oil exports to hold down cooking oil prices after the rupiah collapsed. Cooking oil rose from Rp 1,750 per kg in July 1997 to Rp 5,900 per kg in July 1998 (CIFOR, Casson 2000). The ban was replaced with export taxes of 40%, then 60% in July 1998, cut to 10% by July 1999. CIFOR warns the opening to foreign plantation investment could add pressure on forest cover; in June 1998 state forestry firms were also allowed to turn 30% of their concessions into estate crops. Communities seized back land and attacked estates in 1998; the ministry estimated at least 39,800 ha of plantations looted.
cases.killed_note: CIFOR reports injuries and deaths in clashes between estate workers and communities in 1998 but gives no count.
cases.outcome: CIFOR found new planting fell by a third in 1997-99 because of the crisis, so the forest effects of the foreign-investment opening were not yet clear in 2000.

sources.title: Indonesia Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies, January 15, 1998
The Hesitant Boom: Indonesia's Oil Palm Sub-Sector in an Era of Economic Crisis and Political Change (Occasional Paper 29)
IFIs Update No. 2 (summary of Friends of the Earth, The IMF: Selling the Environment)

cases.confidence_note: The conditions are in the IMF's own memorandum. The main cause of the cooking oil price rise was the rupiah's collapse; the IMF condition removed the ban the government used against it. Forest harm from the foreign-investment opening was a risk, not a measured result, by 2000.

cases.title: Greece 2012 minimum wage cut and bargaining law
cases.point: Syntagma Square, where unions protested during the February 2012 general strike

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The March 2012 Extended Fund Facility request lists the minimum wage cut and bargaining reforms as prior actions (IMF Country Report 12/57).

lenders.name: European Commission and European Central Bank
lenders.role: Co-lenders in the 'troika' program; the conditions sit in the Memorandum of Understanding (Eurofound).

cases.conditions: IMF Country Report 12/57 (March 2012), Greek letter of intent: 'an immediate realignment of the minimum wage level ... by 22 percent', a freeze to the end of the program, and a further 10% cut for under-25s, as a prior action. Also: collective agreements limited to 3 years, after-effects of expired agreements cut to basic pay and four allowances, and an end to arbitration requested by one side only.
cases.community: The gross minimum wage fell from €751.39 to €586.08 a month, and to €426.64 net for under-25s, a 32% cut (Eurofound). Firm-level agreements jumped from an average of 160 a year to 976 in 2012; 74.9% of firm-level contracts after the reform cut base pay, against 3.9% before, and the average base wage in them fell 9.2% (Daouli et al., Journal of Labor Research 2016). Of 826 firm-level agreements with wage terms in 2012, 53% cut base pay, about half of those by more than 20%.
cases.outcome: GSEE held a 48-hour general strike on 10-11 February 2012 and appealed to the Council of State and the ILO. The lower rates stayed until the program ended in 2018. In February 2019 the minimum wage was raised 10.9% and the youth rate abolished, raising pay for about 600,000 people (LSE).

cases.title: Portugal troika labour law changes
cases.point: Lisbon, seat of the government that signed the 2011 program (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The September 2011 letter of intent and Memorandum of Understanding set cuts in severance pay and unemployment benefits.

lenders.name: European Commission and European Central Bank
lenders.role: Co-lenders; the ETUC says the troika insisted on stricter rules for extending collective agreements.

cases.conditions: IMF letter of intent, September 1, 2011: severance for new open-ended contracts 'reduced from 30 to 10 days per year of tenure', capped at 12 months, with the 3-month minimum dropped (the memorandum of economic policies in the same package gives 20 days); maximum unemployment benefit cut to 18 months and capped at 2.5 times the social support index. The May 2011 memorandum also changed rules for extending collective agreements (Addison et al.).
cases.community: From October 2012 sector agreements could be extended to a whole industry only if signatory employers had more than half its workers. Workers covered by newly published agreements fell from 1,894,846 in 2008 to 327,662 in 2012 and 242,676 in 2013, an 87% drop (Addison, Portugal and Vilares, from ministry data). Extended agreements fell from 116 in 2010 to nine in 2013 (ETUC). In seven of ten manufacturing firms studied, managers cut overtime pay on their own (Távora and González).
cases.outcome: In June 2014 the extension rule was loosened for sectors dominated by small firms. Addison et al. argue total coverage under all existing agreements barely moved (90.5% in 2008, 89.2% in 2013) because old agreements stayed in force.

sources.title: Portugal: Letter of Intent, Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies and MoU, September 1, 2011
Unions and Collective Bargaining in the Wake of the Great Recession: Evidence from Portugal
The Functioning of the Troika: A Report from the ETUC
The impact of the crisis on collective bargaining in manufacturing in Portugal

cases.confidence_note: The fall is in new agreements; Addison et al. find total coverage stayed near 90%, while the ETUC puts private-sector coverage at about 1.5 million before the troika and 300,000 in 2012. Sources disagree on how much coverage fell.

cases.title: Romania Social Dialogue Act 2011
cases.point: Bucharest, seat of the government that issued the act (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Romania's December 22, 2010 letter of intent promised to send 'a revised social dialog code and an improved labor code' to parliament after consulting the IMF, World Bank and European Commission.

lenders.name: European Commission
lenders.role: Co-lender; with the IMF it backed the ban on national bargaining and in 2012 pressed the government not to restore labour rights (Trif and Paolucci; ITUC).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Named in the letter of intent as consulted on the labour and social dialogue codes.

cases.conditions: Letter of intent, December 22, 2010: send a revised social dialogue code and labour code to parliament by end-December, to 'increase flexibility' and representativity. Trif and Paolucci: labour market flexibility 'was one of the conditions' for the roughly €20 billion 2010 loan.
cases.community: Law 62/2011 abolished the national collective agreement, made sector deals bind only member firms and only where they employ over half the sector, and required a union to represent over half of a firm's workers (Eurofound). Bargaining coverage fell from 98% in 2010 to 35% in 2011; sector agreements fell from 20 in 2008 to seven in 2014, with only four new ones in 2011-2015; union density fell from about 33% to about 20% (Trif and Paolucci, citing the Ministry of Labour and others).
cases.suppression: The ITUC reports the IMF and Commission privately opposed a 2012 ordinance to restore rights, saying they were concerned about 'loosening procedures' on strikes.
cases.outcome: The government passed the act without a parliamentary vote, in May 2011 (Eurofound). In 2012 the local union threshold was lowered from over 50% to 35%, which the lenders welcomed; national bargaining stayed banned.

cases.title: Ukraine farmland sale ban lifted
cases.point: Verkhovna Rada (parliament), Kyiv, where farmers protested and the law passed

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Lifting the farmland sale ban was one of two main conditions for a new IMF program; funds were held back until the law passed (OSW). IMF chief Georgieva linked faster approval to land reform legislation (Euronews).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The Bretton Woods Project and Oakland Institute say the Bank and IMF pushed creation of a land market; with the EBRD the Bank has lent $1.7 billion to the farm sector.

cases.conditions: Pass a law ending the 2001 ban on selling farmland, plus a banking law, before a new IMF arrangement worth about $8 billion (Euronews; OSW). Parliament voted on March 30-31, 2020.
cases.community: The law opened 41.5 million ha to sale from July 1, 2021: individuals up to 100 ha at first, and from July 2023 companies up to 10,000 ha each; a proposed 33% cap on one buyer's share of land in a local area was dropped (OSW). A February 2020 Razumkov Centre poll found only 19.6% of Ukrainians backed lifting the ban and 64.4% opposed it. The Oakland Institute says about 28% of arable land is held by oligarchs and big agribusinesses.
cases.suppression: During the December 2019 debate, police broke up a farmers' protest outside parliament; 'dozens' were arrested (Oakland Institute).
cases.killed_note: The Oakland Institute reports one death among protesters but gives no name or details.
cases.outcome: The IMF approved a $5 billion Stand-By Arrangement in June 2020. Sales of state land (10.4 million ha) and sales to foreigners stayed banned (OSW).

cases.title: Kenya garment and textile collapse
cases.point: Nairobi garment cluster surveyed by IDE-JETRO (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank and IMF
lenders.role: Requested trade liberalization in Kenya's structural adjustment programs from the 1980s; Kenya began it in the early 1990s (IDE-JETRO). Kenya's trade ministry blamed both for the textile collapse in a 2025 policy (Nation Media).

cases.conditions: Trade liberalization (tariff cuts and import opening) under 1980s-1990s structural adjustment programs, effective from 1994 (IDE-JETRO). No source opened here names the specific loan or tariff figures.
cases.community: Imports of new garments jumped in 1994 and second-hand clothing imports rose from 1997 to about US$40 million in 2001. Real output was roughly halved in the late 1990s. Nairobi garment firms with more than 10 workers fell from 63-74 (1989 University of Nairobi survey) to 48 (2003 IDE survey), a 23-35% fall (IDE-JETRO, Fukunishi).
cases.outcome: In 2025 Kenya's Ministry of Investments, Trade and Industry issued a revival policy blaming the decline on structural adjustment from the mid-1980s.

sources.title: Kenya garment industry chapter (Interim Report 410, ch. 5)
Kenya blames IMF, World Bank for textiles industry collapse

cases.confidence_note: The link is general: IDE-JETRO says the Bank and Fund requested trade liberalization, and the Kenyan government blames them, but no loan document or specific tariff condition was found. IDE notes Kenyan production statistics are unreliable.

cases.title: Egypt Law 96 tenant evictions
cases.point: Al-Mahalla al-Kubra in the Nile Delta, where about 150 farmers were arrested in July 1997 (Amnesty)

lenders.name: IMF and World Bank
lenders.role: Egypt Independent reports the 1990s farm reforms were made under IMF and World Bank pressure. UNRISD (Bush) names USAID and the World Bank as donors behind market-based tenancy.

cases.conditions: Law 96 of 1992 ended rent control on farmland and, after a five-year transition ending in October 1997, let owners evict tenants. No IMF or World Bank document opened here names the law as a condition.
cases.community: Rents rose 7 to 22 times between 1992 and October 1997 (MERIP); Egypt Independent reports LE500 per feddan rising to LE4,000-6,000. The Land Center for Human Rights (LCHR) counts about 904,000 tenants (30% of farmers, about 5.3 million people with families) whose rights were affected; Egypt Independent cites LCHR on about one million farmers evicted. MERIP reports up to 45% of tenants left the land.
cases.suppression: Amnesty reported at least 250 farmers arrested in early July 1997, including 95 in Minya given 15-day detention orders, and earlier detainees reportedly tortured. Human Rights Watch said 'hundreds' were detained and over 150 still held in August 1997.
cases.killed_note: 13 killed and over 60 injured by August 1997, per the Land Center for Human Rights, cited by Human Rights Watch. LCHR later counted about 100 killed in 1997 and 300 more from 1998 to 2004 in land disputes.
cases.outcome: Article 33 promised desert land to evicted tenants, but LCHR says this did not happen, and tenants got no compensation for houses or machinery.
